abstract: Maternal exercise during pregnancy can influence offspring metabolic health, but whether exercise initiated exclusively during lactation has lasting effects is less clear. We investigated the effects of postpartum exercise in chow-fed and high-fat diet (HFD)-fed dams and followed their offspring after weaning. Female C57BL/6J mice consumed chow or a 60% HFD before mating and throughout lactation. Beginning on postpartum day 1, dams were assigned to sedentary or treadmill-exercise conditions until weaning on day 25. Offspring were maintained on chow and assessed longitudinally for body mass, body composition, glucose tolerance, and insulin tolerance through adulthood. Postpartum exercise reduced maternal adiposity and improved maternal glucose tolerance, with effects observed in both chow- and HFD-fed dams. Maternal postpartum exercise was associated with altered offspring growth trajectories and body composition, with effects becoming more apparent with advancing age. Glucose tolerance also improved with maternal exercise in adult male and female offspring, whereas insulin tolerance did not differ significantly among maternal treatment groups. These findings suggest that maternal exercise during lactation is associated with long-term differences in offspring metabolic health that persist long after cessation of the maternal intervention and become increasingly apparent in adulthood. Our findings expand the exercise-responsive window for developmental metabolic programming beyond pregnancy and support lactation as a potentially modifiable period during which maternal physical activity may influence long-term offspring metabolic health.
